headline: Cambridge Dictionary's word of the year is 'human'

sources.title: 'Human' revealed as Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year for 2026 (CNN)
Cambridge Dictionary chooses 'human' as word of the year in response to AI fears (AP via OPB)
Would AI have come up with a better word of the year than the Cambridge Dictionary? (CBC News)
Cambridge Dictionary pushes back on AI with 'human' as 2026 Word of the Year (Rappler)

chunks.text: The Cambridge Dictionary has chosen an old, simple word as its [[word of the year]] for 2026: "human." The British dictionary announced its choice on November 18, 2026. It said the word {{sums up}} a year of [[global debate]] about artificial intelligence, or AI. "Human" {{goes back}} to the 1450s. It means having the [[qualities]], [[faults]] and feelings that people have, [[as opposed to]] gods, animals or machines.

verbs.correct: To show the main idea of something
verbs.wrong: To change the meaning of a word
verbs.why: This photo sums up our whole vacation. One short sentence often sums up a long report. The dictionary said "human" sums up a year of global debate about AI.

verbs.correct: To have existed since an earlier time
verbs.wrong: To be printed in a newer book
verbs.why: This old song goes back to the 1800s. Our family bakery goes back four generations. The word "human" goes back to the 1450s.

chunks.text: Dictionaries usually pick a new word, or an older word that has {{taken on}} a new meaning. "Human" is the second kind. AI tools can now quickly {{churn out}} text and images. So terms such as "human-made" and "human-written" have {{caught on}}. These [[compound words]] {{set a person's work apart}} from anything made by AI. In a [[marketplace]] full of AI content, the dictionary says, human work now suggests care, [[judgment]] and the small [[imperfections]] that make something feel real.

verbs.correct: To begin to have something new
verbs.wrong: To be spelled in a new way
verbs.why: Words often take on new meanings over time. A simple song often takes on a deeper meaning at a funeral. The word "human" has taken on a new meaning in the age of AI.

verbs.correct: To make a lot of something quickly
verbs.wrong: To print something on old paper
verbs.why: This factory churns out thousands of toys a day. Some writers churn out three books a year. AI tools can now quickly churn out text and images.
New dance styles catch on fast with teenagers. Some fashions never catch on outside big cities. Terms such as "human-made" have caught on.

verbs.wrong: To give something a lower price
verbs.why: Good service sets this small hotel apart from the others. Her strong voice sets her apart from other singers. Terms such as "human-written" set a person's work apart from anything made by AI.

chunks.text: The dictionary said it studied [[internet trends]] and what people {{look up}} online. Its lexicographer, an expert who writes dictionaries, said people fear what they may lose when they {{hand their thinking over}} to machines. The dictionary quoted an AI [[pioneer]] and Nobel Prize winner who had {{spoken out}} about AI. He said he was willing to "choose humans." Famous people are {{pushing back}} against AI [[deepfakes]], fake images and voices that seem real. Stars such as Taylor Swift have used [[trademarks]], a kind of [[legal protection]], to guard their images and voices.

verbs.correct: To find a fact in a book or online
verbs.wrong: To tear a page from a book
verbs.why: I look up new words on my phone. Many students look up the answers online. The dictionary studied what people look up online.

verbs.correct: To give control of something to another
verbs.wrong: To print a long list of new words
verbs.why: Some managers hand big decisions over to their teams. Many owners hand their shops over to their children. The dictionary's expert said people fear what they may lose when they hand their thinking over to machines.

verbs.wrong: To sell a machine to a school
verbs.why: Many nurses speak out about long work hours. Students often speak out when school costs rise. The dictionary quoted an AI pioneer and Nobel Prize winner who had spoken out about AI.

verbs.correct: To show that you oppose something
verbs.wrong: To sell your image to a company
verbs.why: Workers push back when a company cuts their pay. Parents often push back against new school rules. Famous people are pushing back against AI deepfakes.

chunks.text: Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates {{weighed in}} on the choice. He said AI is making people think harder about what it means to be human. "Human" {{won out}} over four other [[finalists]]. One was "agent," an AI system that can [[make decisions]] [[on its own]]. In 2023, Cambridge picked "hallucinate," a word for when AI tools {{make up}} information.

verbs.correct: To add your opinion to a discussion
verbs.wrong: To pay for a new research project
verbs.why: My sister always weighs in when we plan a trip. Doctors often weigh in on new health rules. Bill Gates weighed in on the choice of "human."

verbs.wrong: To be read aloud at a school
verbs.why: In my house, pizza usually wins out over salad. Good ideas usually win out at our meetings. The word "human" won out over four other finalists.

verbs.correct: To invent something that is not true
verbs.wrong: To count the pages in a book
verbs.why: Children often make up stories about their day. Some people make up excuses when they are late. Cambridge picked "hallucinate" in 2023, a word for when AI tools make up information.

vocab.def: To show the main idea of something
ex: That one word sums up how I feel about my job.
For many fans, that last game sums up the whole season.
Her short speech summed up what the team had learned.

vocab.def: To have existed since an earlier time
ex: This tradition goes back hundreds of years.
Their friendship goes back to elementary school.
The town's main church goes back to the 1700s.

vocab.def: To begin to have something new
ex: The room takes on a warm color at sunset.
After the storm, the old photo took on special meaning for her.
His voice took on a serious tone.

vocab.def: To make a lot of something quickly
ex: The studio churns out a new movie every month.
That bakery churns out hundreds of loaves each morning.
The printer churned out page after page.
The new app caught on quickly at our school.
Electric bikes are starting to catch on in my city.
I never thought that song would catch on.
Her kindness sets her apart from other managers.
What sets this phone apart from the cheaper ones?
Fresh bread sets that restaurant apart.

vocab.def: To find a fact in a book or online
ex: I had to look up the address before we left.
She looked up the bus times on her phone.
If you don't know the word, look it up.

vocab.def: To give control of something to another
ex: He handed the business over to his daughter.
The mayor will hand control of the project over to a new team.
I don't want to hand my decisions over to anyone else.
She spoke out about unfair pay at her company.
More parents are speaking out about school safety.
It takes courage to speak out in a small town.

vocab.def: To show that you oppose something
ex: Neighbors pushed back against the plan for a new parking lot.
The workers are pushing back against longer hours.
When the rent went higher, the tenants pushed back.

vocab.def: To add your opinion to a discussion
ex: Everyone at the table weighed in on the plan.
The coach weighed in on the new rule.
Would you like to weigh in before we decide?
We looked at two apartments, and the cheaper one won out.
In the end, the simple design won out.
Her idea won out over all the others.

vocab.def: To invent something that is not true
ex: He made up a story about losing his homework.
Don't believe him, because he is making that up.
She made up a reason to leave the party early.

wordDefs.def: A word chosen because it shows what a year was like
ex: Our teacher asked us to choose a word of the year for our class.
Each December, I think about what my word of the year would be.
The radio show asked listeners for their word of the year.

wordDefs.def: A discussion about an issue among people around the world
ex: Climate change is part of a global debate.
The new law started a global debate about privacy.
There is a global debate about how children should use phones.
Patience and honesty are important qualities in a teacher.
What qualities do you want in a friend?
She has many good qualities.

wordDefs.def: Weak or bad parts of a person's character
ex: We all have our faults.
He loves his wife in spite of her faults.
One of my faults is that I talk too much.

wordDefs.def: Used to show that two things are different
ex: I prefer trains, as opposed to buses.
We need facts, as opposed to guesses.
She works in the morning, as opposed to at night.

wordDefs.def: Words made by joining two or more words
ex: "Sunflower" and "toothbrush" are compound words.
English has many compound words.
The children learned to spot compound words in the story.

wordDefs.def: The world of buying and selling
ex: Small shops struggle in a crowded marketplace.
The new phone must compete in a busy marketplace.
Online sellers have changed the marketplace.

wordDefs.def: The ability to make good decisions
ex: A good doctor needs sound judgment.
I trust your judgment on this.
Being tired can affect your judgment.

wordDefs.def: Small marks or faults in something
ex: Handmade cups often have small imperfections.
The jacket is cheaper because of tiny imperfections.
I like the imperfections in old wooden tables.

wordDefs.def: Things that quickly become popular online
ex: My daughter follows all the latest internet trends.
Some internet trends are gone in a week.
Companies watch internet trends to plan their ads.

wordDefs.def: One of the first people to work in a new field
ex: She was a pioneer of heart surgery.
He is known as a pioneer of electric cars.
The school honored a pioneer in women's sports.

wordDefs.def: Names, images or signs that the law lets only the owner use
ex: The company owns several trademarks.
Logos are often protected as trademarks.
You can't use other companies' trademarks on your products.

wordDefs.def: Help from the law that keeps someone or something safe
ex: Renters have legal protection in many states.
New inventions may need legal protection.
Workers asked for stronger legal protection.

wordDefs.def: Fake images, videos or voices made by computers to seem real
ex: Deepfakes can make it hard to trust online videos.
The class learned how to spot deepfakes.
Some deepfakes copy a person's voice.

wordDefs.def: The last people or things left in a competition
ex: The judges chose three finalists for the prize.
All the finalists gave excellent speeches.
Our school had two finalists in the science fair.
Managers make decisions every day.
It is hard to make decisions when you are tired.
Teenagers want to make decisions for themselves.

wordDefs.def: Without help or control from anyone
ex: The door closes on its own.
This vacuum cleaner works on its own.
The small plant grew on its own.

mainIdea.s: Cambridge named a very old word as its top pick for 2026 because AI has people asking what makes us different from machines. Terms like "human-made" now show that a person did the work.
mainIdea.why: The word sums up a year of debate about AI. Terms such as "human-written" have caught on and set a person's work apart.

mainIdea.s: The dictionary picked "human" since its experts believe AI will soon replace most writers and artists. Its editors want readers to stop using these tools and buy only handmade goods.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the choice reflects a debate about AI. The dictionary does not tell people to stop using AI, and it says terms like "human-made" have caught on.

mainIdea.s: A British publisher has removed hundreds of old entries from its pages to make room for new computer terms. Teachers complain that students will now know less about the history of English.
mainIdea.why: Nothing was removed. Cambridge chose "human" as its word of the year, and the word goes back to the 1450s.

tf.s: The Cambridge Dictionary says "human" sums up a year of debate about AI.
tf.why: The dictionary chose the word because of the global debate about what AI means for people.

tf.s: The word "human" goes back only a few years.
tf.why: It is a very old word. It goes back to the 1450s.

tf.s: Terms like "human-written" make people's work and AI work seem the same.
tf.why: These terms do the opposite. They set a person's work apart from anything made by AI.

tf.s: Terms such as "human-made" have caught on as AI content has spread.
tf.why: AI tools can churn out content very quickly, so people now say when a person made something.

tf.s: Some famous people are pushing back against AI deepfakes.
tf.why: Stars such as Taylor Swift have used trademarks to guard their images and voices.

tf.s: The dictionary's expert said nobody worries about handing thinking over to AI.
tf.why: He said people fear what they may lose when they hand their thinking over to machines.

lines.text: Did you see the Cambridge Dictionary's word of the year? It's "human."
Human? That word {{goes back}} centuries. Why pick it now?
Because of AI. They say it {{sums up}} the whole debate about people and machines.
Right. AI can {{churn out}} content so fast, and now "human-made" has {{caught on}}.
So an old word has {{taken on}} a new meaning.
Exactly. It {{sets your work apart}} from what a machine makes.
[[When you think about it]], that's strange. Now we have to say a person made something.
People want [[the human touch]]. [[You can tell]] when someone really cared about the work.
Can you, though? What about deepfakes?
Good question. Taylor Swift and other stars are {{pushing back}} with trademarks on their images and voices.
[[I'd do the same]]. And AI still {{makes up}} information, right?
Sometimes, yes. That's why "hallucinate" was the pick in 2023.
What else was on the list this time?
Good. I'd hate to {{hand my thinking over}} to an agent.

expressions.def: Used to react to something new that shows how much life is changing
ex: My fridge just sent me a message. Welcome to the future.

expressions.def: Used before saying something that becomes clear after some thought
ex: When you think about it, phones have changed everything.

expressions.def: The warm, personal quality that comes from a real person
ex: Our doctor has the human touch.
A handwritten note adds the human touch.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is easy to notice or understand
ex: You can tell she loves her job.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone's choice is right and you would make it too
ex: She asked for more pay? I'd do the same.
